lead: Scaling means building the same circuit with smaller transistors. If the lengths, the oxide and the supply voltage all shrink by the same factor S, the electric fields inside the device stay the same, the transistor still works, each gate gets faster and uses less power, and S² more gates fit in the same area. When the voltage cannot follow the lengths, power density climbs, and when the channel gets very short the drain starts to control it: the short-channel effects. This chapter puts numbers on both, with the power consumption of a gate.
prereq: You need: the square law from MOSFET I-V characteristics and device equations and gate capacitance from MOSFET capacitances and parasitic resistances.

blocks.text: Pick S > 1. Divide L, W, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> by S and multiply the doping N<sub>A</sub> by S, so the depletion widths shrink with the device. Field = voltage/length is unchanged. Some books call this full scaling or Dennard scaling, after the 1974 paper that set it out.
That last row is the prize: S² more gates on a chip, each 1/S faster, for the same watts per mm².

If V<sub>DD</sub> stays fixed while the lengths shrink by S, the field rises by S. In the square-law model the current rises by S (C<sub>ox</sub> up by S, V<sub>ov</sub> unchanged), delay falls as 1/S², power per gate rises as S and power density as S³. In practice velocity saturation limits the current gain, but the heat problem remains.
The power a CMOS gate consumes has three parts:

items: Dynamic (switching) power P = α·CL·VDD²·f, where CL is the load capacitance, f the clock frequency and α the activity factor (the fraction of cycles in which the output rises). Each rise draws CL·VDD² from the supply.
Short-circuit power, while the input passes through the middle and both nMOS and pMOS conduct briefly.
Static power VDD·Ileak from leakage, which flows even when nothing switches (see Leakage and subthreshold conduction).

blocks.text: The power-delay product PDP = Pavg × tp, the energy per switching event, compares logic families fairly: a gate that is slow because it saves power is not rewarded twice. Supply voltage fell from 5 V towards 1 V, but VT cannot fall much below about 0.3 V without leakage exploding. So from the mid-2000s VDD has stayed near 1 V, power density has risen, and chips have used more cores instead of faster clocks. Inverter-level power is worked further in the topic Static and dynamic power dissipation.
Once L is comparable to the source and drain depletion widths, the drain field reaches the source end of the channel and the gate no longer controls the channel alone.

items: VT roll-off: source and drain depletion regions take a share of the charge under the gate, so the gate holds less and VT falls as L falls.
DIBL (drain-induced barrier lowering): a high VDS lowers the barrier at the source, so VT falls as VDS rises, quoted in mV/V. Off current rises and the saturated curve gains slope.
Punch-through: at high VDS the source and drain depletion regions merge under the channel, and current flows whatever the gate voltage. Halo (pocket) implants and heavier doping push it back.
GIDL and gate tunnelling: thin oxides and sharp drain fields add leakage paths, covered in Leakage and subthreshold conduction.

sections.h3: Hot carriers, LDD, NBTI and oxide breakdown

blocks.text: Hot carriers: the lateral field peaks near the drain; some electrons gain enough energy to enter the oxide or break bonds at the interface, so VT drifts and gm falls over years. A lightly doped drain (LDD) puts an n⁻ extension between channel and n⁺ drain, spreading the voltage over a longer distance and lowering the peak field, at the cost of some series resistance.

NBTI (negative bias temperature instability): a pMOS held with its gate low at high temperature builds interface traps, so |VT| slowly rises and the gate slows; it partly recovers when the stress is removed. Oxide breakdown (time-dependent dielectric breakdown): a thin oxide under field slowly forms a conducting path and fails, which limits how high VDD can go for a given tox.

examples.question: A gate in a 0.25 µm process drives C = 10 fF at V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V and switches once per cycle (α = 1) at 100 MHz. The process is scaled to 0.125 µm with constant-field rules. Find the dynamic power before and after, and the change in power density.
steps: After: C = 10/2 = 5 fF, V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5/2 = 1.25 V, delay halves so f = 200 MHz.
Ratio 6.25/1.5625 = 4 = S². Area per gate also falls by S² = 4, so power density is unchanged.
examples.answer: 6.25 µW before, 1.56 µW after; power per gate falls by 4 and power density stays the same.

examples.question: Scale the same gate by S = 2 but keep V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V (constant-voltage scaling, square-law device). Find the new clock, power, power density and energy per cycle C·V<sub>DD</sub>², and compare with the constant-field case.
steps: C = 5 fF; delay scales as 1/S² = 1/4, so f = 400 MHz.
P = 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 2.5² × 400 × 10⁶ = 12.5 µW, twice the original (factor S).
Area falls by 4, so power density rises by 2 × 4 = 8 = S³.
Energy per cycle: original 10 fF × 2.5² = 62.5 fJ; constant voltage 5 × 6.25 = 31.25 fJ; constant field 5 × 1.25² = 7.81 fJ (1/S³).
examples.answer: 400 MHz, 12.5 µW, eight times the power density; energy per cycle 31.25 fJ against 7.81 fJ with constant-field scaling.

traps: Constant-field scaling keeps power density at 1; constant-voltage scaling raises it as S³.
Constant-field delay scales as 1/S; 1/S² is the constant-voltage result.
DIBL lowers V<sub>T</sub> while the gate still controls the channel; punch-through is the loss of gate control.
V<sub>T</sub> roll-off (V<sub>T</sub> falls as L falls) and the body effect (V<sub>T</sub> rises with V<sub>SB</sub>) are different knobs.
Dynamic power uses V<sub>DD</sub>², so halving the supply alone cuts it by four.

quiz.q: State the constant-field scaling rules for L, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>T</sub> and N<sub>A</sub>.
quiz.a: L, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> divide by S; N<sub>A</sub> multiplies by S.

quiz.q: Why does constant-field scaling keep power density constant but constant-voltage scaling does not?
quiz.a: Constant field: power per gate 1/S² and area 1/S², ratio 1. Constant voltage: power per gate S while area is 1/S², ratio S³.

quiz.q: C = 20 fF, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, f = 200 MHz, α = 1. Scale by S = 3 with constant-field rules; find the new dynamic power.
V<sub>T</sub> = 0.30 V at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.1 V and 0.20 V at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.1 V. Find the DIBL.
quiz.a: ΔV<sub>T</sub> = 100 mV over ΔV<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V: DIBL = 100 mV/V.

quiz.q: What does an LDD structure do, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: It adds a lightly doped extension between the channel and the drain, lowering the peak lateral field and hot-carrier damage. It adds series resistance, so drive current falls a little.

quiz.q: Why did V<sub>DD</sub> stop falling near 1 V even though transistors kept shrinking?
quiz.a: To keep speed, V<sub>T</sub> must fall with V<sub>DD</sub>, but each 60 to 100 mV drop in V<sub>T</sub> raises subthreshold leakage about ten times. Leakage power set a floor on V<sub>T</sub>, and so on V<sub>DD</sub>; power density then rose and clock speeds levelled off.

beyond: After constant-field scaling ended, density kept rising through strained silicon, high-k metal gates, FinFETs and now gate-all-around nanosheets. The International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS) publishes the projected dimensions and voltages of future nodes. Search for "Dennard scaling breakdown" and "dark silicon".
